- 待核查：当前版本、模型、池/区域、驱动/CUDA、gate/deny/pin实际状态及实时遥测；当前是否仍存在长prefill回退，或排队/饱和等其他原因。

Title: Northwind Analytics - technical deep dive: tail latency + KV cache behavior

AUTO-GENERATED SUMMARY
Northwind described burst-driven p99 latency spikes in chat-style workloads with mixed prompt lengths, plus occasional GPU OOM / request shedding on their current stack. Redwood walked through how KV cache allocation patterns and fragmentation can create tail latency under churn, especially when long-lived sessions coexist with short requests and cancellation/retry behavior. Redwood outlined planned runtime improvements: fragmentation measurement, budgeted compaction integrated with the scheduler, and tier-aware eviction (LRU-ish) with kill-switches and observability. Discussion covered what signals to capture (decode vs prefill timing, allocator arena health, bytes moved), and how to run a benchmark that reproduces Northwind’s traffic shape.

TOPICS
- What “tail latency” looks like in mixed-length decode workloads
- KV cache basics (pages/blocks), long-lived allocations, churn, cancellations
- Fragmentation: why it happens, what it costs, why it triggers at the wrong time
- Compaction: incremental vs background, budgets, scheduler integration
- Eviction policy: tier-aware + LRU, pinned sessions, prefix caching interactions
- Guardrails: backpressure, kill-switch, rollback criteria, metrics
- Benchmark ask + what Redwood needs from Northwind

QUESTIONS (captured)
- Can Redwood separate prefill latency from decode latency per request? (Yes, and we can share how we instrument it.)
- How does compaction avoid stalling decode? (Budgeted moves tied to scheduler boundaries; can pause under load.)
- Does eviction affect correctness or output stability? (No correctness change; could impact cache hit rates, which affects latency/cost.)
- Can Dedicated/VPC reduce tail by avoiding noisy neighbors? (Often helps, but fragmentation is still a per-process issue; runtime fixes matter either way.)

Summary (auto-generated)
Northwind asked for a deeper walkthrough of how Redwood selects GPU kernels at runtime, specifically around long-context summarization workloads and heterogeneous GPU fleets. Redwood explained kernel auto-selection v2 signals (model family/arch tags, sequence-length regime, GPU SKU normalization), fallback hierarchy, determinism guarantees, and rollout safety controls (feature gates, per-model allow/deny lists, rapid rollback, manual pinning). The group aligned on running a small benchmark matrix on A100 and L40S, with realistic prompt/decode distributions and tail latency monitoring.

Topics (auto-generated)
- Kernel selection: what it is, where it runs, and what inputs it uses
- GPU SKU mapping (A100 variants, MIG, cloud instance naming)
- Long-context performance: prefill vs decode regime and tail latency risk

- Benchmark plan + what data Northwind needs to provide

Questions (auto-generated)
- How do you prevent non-deterministic selection decisions across replicas?
- Can we force/pin a kernel for a specific model and GPU in Dedicated?

[00:03] Priya Nair: Yep, loud and clear.

evidence.title: Cross-sku MIG clock interlock: kernel prioritization and attention tiling for H100/L40S/A10
evidence.text:
description:
Background: multi-tenant inference workloads on H100/L40S/A10 show volatile tail latency during MIG consolidation and clock domain shifts. Current kernel selection heuristics assume static clock/perf profiles and do not account for transient P2P/NVLink contention or mixed quantized/FP16 execution paths. Goal: implement a cross-sku clock-interlock and kernel prioritization layer plus an attention-tiling policy that adapts prefill/decode scheduling to MIG partitioning and real-time clock governors. Success metrics: 95th percentile latency reduction of 15-25% on mixed small/long-sequence workloads across MIG partitions; token cost neutral or improved; no regression in throughput for long-batch offline workloads.

acceptance_criteria:
Kernel router uses live clock and MIG fragmentation signals to rank candidate kernels before scheduling
Attention tiler adjusts tile size and KV alignment to reduce L2 thrash on L40S without increasing decode latency > 5%
Prefill/decode interleave window introduced to avoid clock-rebalance stalls during MIG reconfigure and reduces 95th latency by >=15% in benchmark suite
Automated telemetry demonstrates correct fallback to a quantized-kernel-fusion path on A10 when H100/L40S capacity constrained
End-to-end e2e perf tests and canary on dedicated pool show no increase in error rate or CPU OOMs

work_notes:
2025-01-18: RFC written; linked design doc with microbenchmarks. Trade-offs considered: aggressive prefill batching vs latency-sensitive interleaving. Decision: hybrid interleaving with dynamic cutover thresholds.
2025-01-22: Infra experiment on staging with synthetic chat workload; observed 28% 95th latency spike when MIG fragmentation >60% during background training noise.
2025-01-25: Implemented clock-interlock event listener in runtime and exposed telemetry flag runtime.clock_interlock.enabled (off by default).
2025-01-29: Prototyped kernel-ranking heuristic that weights (kernel_peak_bw, current_device_clock, nvlink_util, mig_fragment_score). Initial synthetic results: 12% 95th reduction on H100-only trials.
2025-02-01: L40S attention tiler patch submitted; adjusts attn_tile to favor smaller tiles when L2 miss rate > 18%. PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4921
2025-02-03: End-to-end benchmark ran against mixed H100/L40S/A10 pool with prefill+decode interleave window set to 40ms; 95th improved by 17% and token cost decreased 3% on median. Noted small throughput regression on long-batch profiles (~4%).
Next steps: add NVLink P2P fallback handshake to kernel router; integrate autoswitch thresholds from telemetry; create canary rollout plan for dedicated customers and a gated feature flag for runtime-1.21 release.

risks_and_mitigations:
Risk: aggressive kernel switching can increase warmup overhead. Mitigation: add hysteresis and min residency time per kernel selection.
Risk: L40S micro-tiling may regress throughput on long static batches. Mitigation: enable tiler only when L2 miss + latency SLO signals are present.
Risk: MIG reconfigure race during runtime may cause transient errors. Mitigation: gate reconfigure events via interlock and drain inflight prefill windows before topology changes.

qa_plan:
Add unit tests for kernel router ranking weights and simulated clock events
Run full perf suite on multi-sku lab (H100/L40S/A10) with and without background NVSwitch load
Canary rollout to dedicated pool group 'perf-canary-02' with telemetry thresholds for automatic rollback

What’s shipping:
- Runtime 1.21 includes kernel auto-selection v2 behind feature gates (default OFF unless allowlisted).

- Safe staged rollout with rapid rollback and per-model/per-region overrides.

- Model-family classifier integration (architecture tags / variants).
- Seq-length bucketing + prefill/decode regime heuristics.
- GPU SKU-aware kernel registry + normalization (including variants/MIG where applicable).
- Guardrail: auto-disable v2 on known-unstable driver/CUDA combos.

- Decision rules are explicit + debuggable; telemetry captures “why” (features + candidate set).
- Fallback hierarchy prevents hard failures when a preferred kernel is missing/unstable.
- Determinism: selection depends only on declared inputs; replay tests guarantee identical selection.

1) Global gate: kernel_selection_v2.enabled (per env)

- Enabled only for explicit allowlisted model families + GPU SKUs in hosted canary clusters.
- Dedicated/Private: opt-in only (customer readiness review required).

- Bench matrix coverage complete for key model families + seq distributions + SKUs

- Add 1–2 regions; expand allow

- **Sequence-length regime** (prefill-heavy, decode-heavy, mixed; plus long-context buckets)
- **GPU SKU** (e.g., A100 vs H100 vs L40S; including normalization of common cloud instance naming)

- chosen kernel
- candidate set (capped)
- feature vector (model family, seq bucket, gpu sku)
- fallback reason (if applicable)

- Force kernel selection for reproductions and customer escalations.
- Dump selection traces locally (or in canary pods) for triage.

[01:03] Markus Klein: Makes sense. Omar, do you wanna start with the “what is kernel selection” for us, like the two-minute overview?

[01:10] Omar El-Sayed: Sure. So, in our runtime we have multiple kernel implementations for key parts of attention and related ops. Depending on model architecture and workload regime, different kernels win. Kernel auto-selection is the module that picks, for a given request, which kernel variant to run.

[01:27] Omar El-Sayed: In v2 specifically, we key selection on three buckets of signals: one, model family/architecture tags (like Llama-style vs Mistral-style, Qwen variants, Gemma-ish), two, sequence-length regime which we treat separately for prefill vs decode behavior, and three, GPU SKU, because H100 vs A100 vs L40S can change the winner.

[01:51] Priya Nair: When you say “request”, do you literally decide per request? Or per model load, like at startup?

[01:57] Yuki Sato: Good question. We decide at request time, but in practice we cache decisions. The selector outputs a decision based on a normalized feature vector. Most of those are stable for many requests: model id + gpu sku + seq bucket. So it’s more like “per regime,” not every time doing heavy computation.

[02:18] Danielle Chen: And your v1 did what?

[02:21] Yuki Sato: v1 was simpler, basically a mostly static mapping keyed on model class and a couple hard-coded thresholds. It didn’t account for SKU differences well, and it treated sequence length too coarsely. It worked for the middle of the distribution but we saw edge cases on long context.

[02:39] Omar El-Sayed: And also v1 had weaker observability. So when you got a latency spike, you couldn’t easily answer “which kernel did we pick” without attaching a profiler.

[02:49] Alex Romero: So v2 is rules? Or some ML thing?

[02:53] Yuki Sato: Rules. We debated a learned scorer, but for safety and explainability and rollback, we landed on rule-based with explicit fallbacks. It’s still a “scoring” concept internally, but it’s deterministic rules and precedence, not a trained model.

[03:10] Priya Nair: Deterministic… like, identical inputs always produce identical output kernel choice?

[03:15] Yuki Sato: Yes. Given the same model metadata, same GPU normalized SKU, same seq bucket inputs, you get the same selection. We’ve added replay tests to ensure that. We also version the rules so if we change thresholds, it’s tracked.

[03:30] Tom Bowers: What about multi-tenant? Like if another customer is running something weird, does it influence our selection?

[03:35] Omar El-Sayed: No. There’s no global learning. The only “dynamic” input can be scheduler hints about observed seq distribution, but those are local to the pool and still deterministic given the hint input. And you can disable that if you want.

[03:49] Ethan Park: Also from the control plane side, for Dedicated you can lock policy. You can say “always use v1 selector” or “use v2 only for these models.” There’s no cross-account mixing.

[04:01] Danielle Chen: Let’s go into the seq bucket thing. Because our problem is long context. How do you bucket?

[04:07] Yuki Sato: We extract prompt length (prefill tokens) and also we estimate expected decode length using either the max_tokens setting or observed from recent traffic. Then we classify into regimes.

[04:19] Yuki Sato: Simplifying a bit: short, medium, long context for prefill; and small vs large decode. For prefill, long context triggers kernels optimized for memory bandwidth and larger tile sizes. Issue summary
- Customer reports p99 latency regression for long-context summarization workloads immediately after we enabled Runtime 1.21 canary on their Dedicated pool. Regression appears only for long-context requests (>= ~16k prompt tokens) and only on NVIDIA L40S.

Impact
- Customer-visible tail latency increase on long-context routes.
- Reported baseline (Runtime 1.20 / selector v1): p99 ~4.8–5.4s @ ~20k prompt tokens, 256–512 decode tokens.
- After canary (Runtime 1.21 / selector v2 enabled): p99 ~8.9–10.6s for same workload; p50/p90 mostly unchanged.
- No correctness issues reported. Error rate stable.

Customer context
- Northwind Analytics uses Redwood Dedicated for long-context summarization (document ingestion + map-reduce style prompts). Workload is bursty but within reserved throughput.

Environment
- Dedicated pool: nw-analytics-ded-01
- Region: us-east
- GPU SKU: NVIDIA L40S (SM89)
- Driver/CUDA: 550.54.14 / CUDA 12.4

evidence.title: Runtime 1.21 Release Notes: Kernel Auto-Selection v2
evidence.text:
n cost is in the **single-digit microseconds** range, and sampling-controlled telemetry overhead is negligible at default settings.

Performance regressions should be treated as a **P0** if they increase p99 tail latency beyond rollout budgets (see SLO gates / dashboards).

---

## Compatibility Notes
- Supported GPU families in rollout scope: **A100, H100, L40S**.
- MIG: supported, but SKU normalization is strict; ensure the runtime reports a normalized `gpu_sku` consistent with the control plane rules.
- Private deployments pinned to constrained GPU types should validate with the benchmark matrix before enabling v2 globally.

---

## Known Limitations / Risks
1) **Long-context misclassification risk (prefill-heavy)**
   - Very long prefill requests (e.g., summarization with large context windows) are sensitive to incorrect bucketing.
   - If you observe tail spikes concentrated in long-context routes, disable v2 for the affected model(s) and region, then collect selection traces.

2) **Driver/CUDA guardrails**
   - Selector v2 is automatically disabled on specific driver/CUDA combinations that have not completed validation.
   - If you are running a nonstandard driver stack (common in some on-prem installs), confirm you are not implicitly falling back to v1.

3) **Telemetry cardinality**
   - New fields can increase metric cardinality if dashboards are queried without the recommended grouping limits.
   - Follow the dashboard spec for safe group-bys (model family / SKU / seq bucket) and avoid raw model-id group-bys unless sampled and capped.

4) **Kernel availability differences by SKU**
   - Some optimized kernels are SKU-specific. v2’s fallback rules are explicit, but you may see different kernel distributions between A100 and H100 under identical traffic.

---

## Rollout / Enablement Guidance
Recommended staged rollout order:
1. Enable v2 in **Hosted canary** for a small model allowlist.
2. Expand allowlist by model family + SKU cohorts (monitor p95/p99 and error rates).
3. Enable in **Dedicated pools** with explicit customer opt-in and documented rollback contact.
4. Promote to broader GA once SLO gates are green for at least one full traffic cycle.

Default enablement approach:
- Start with `kernel_selection.v2.model_allowlist` and keep a conservative denylist for known-sensitive long-context models until validated.

---

## Rollback Instructions (Fast Path)
If you suspect a latency regression, elevated error rate, or unexpected kernel distribution shift, roll back v2 using the smallest-scoped change that resolves impact.

### Hosted / Dedicated (control plane gate)
1. Disable v2 for the affected scope (start with model + region):
   - Set `kernel_selection.v2.enabled=false` (scoped) OR remove the model from the v2 allowlist.
2. Confirm hot reload applied:
   - Verify the selector mode in runtime logs: `kernel_selection_mode=v1` (or `v2 disabled by gate`).
3. Validate recovery:
   - Monitor p95/p99 latency and error rate panels in the Kernel Selection v2 rollout dashboards.
   - Confirm kernel distribution shifts back to expected v1 baselines.

### Private (customer-managed runtime config)
1. Set `kernel_selection.v2.enabled=false` and/or `kernel_selection.mode=v1` in `runtime.yaml`.
2. Restart the runtime service (or reload config if supported in the deployment).
3. Validate with the customer’s canary route:
   - Compare p99 latency for long-context traffic before/after.

### If immediate mitigation is required
- Pin a kernel only as a temporary measure:
  - Use `--force-kernel=<kernel_id>` (or equivalent config) for the impacted route/model while investigating.
  - Open a follow-up issue to remove the pin once denylist or thresholds are corrected.

---

## Troubleshooting Checklist
When filing an issue or escalating to oncall/runtime-kernels, include:
- Model id + model family
- GPU SKU (normalized) + whether MIG is used
- Driver/CUDA version tuple
- Workload description (prefill-heavy vs decode-heavy; typical context lengths)
- Selection traces (`--dump-kernel-selection`) for 20–50 representative requests
- Dashboard links: latency deltas + selection distribution by SKU/seq bucket

---

- Runtime Kernels: **Hiro Tanaka**, **Yuki Sato**
- Perf/correctness guardrails: **Noah Patel**
- Tail latency + observability: **Omar El-Sayed**, **Allison Grant**
- Control-plane feature gates: **Ethan Park**
- Release train: **Connor O'Brien**

For operational procedures and scoped overrides, follow: **Kernel Selection v2 Override and Rollback Runbook** (linked above).

evidence.title: Kernel Auto-Selection v2 — Override and Rollback Runbook
evidence.text:
## Purpose
This runbook describes how oncall can safely override or roll back **Kernel Auto-Selection v2** ("selector v2") when it causes tail-latency regressions, stability issues, or correctness risks. It covers:
- Disabling v2 by **model**, **GPU SKU**, and/or **region** (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)
- Pinning a specific kernel (temporary mitigation)
- Safe rollback procedure (fast + staged)
- Validation steps using dashboards and logs

**Primary goals:** restore p95/p99 latency and error rates to baseline while preserving correctness and preventing fleet-wide disruption.

---

## Scope / when to use
Use this runbook when any of the following are true during canary or production:
- p99 latency regression attributed to kernel selection (common: long-context prefill misclassification)
- Elevated runtime errors (CUDA illegal memory access, miscompiled kernel, launch failures) correlated with a chosen kernel/SKU
- Throughput instability or jitter that correlates with selection distribution changes
- Customer escalation requiring immediate mitigation (Dedicated/Private pools with constrained SKUs)

**Do not use** this runbook for general GPU/node instability, scheduler overload, or non-kernel runtime crashes unless kernel selection has been implicated.

---

## Ownership / escalation
**Oncall owns mitigation**, Runtime Kernels owns root cause.

- Runtime Oncall: #eng-oncall (primary)
- Runtime Kernels: #eng-runtime (paging if rollback required)
- SRE: #eng-sre (paging if SLO breach / incident)
- Releases: #eng-releases (if changes impact runtime 1.21 rollout windows)

Escalate immediately if:
- Any correctness regression suspected (bad outputs, determinism broken)
- Crash-looping exceeds 2% of pods in a region/pool
- You need to disable v2 globally in Hosted prod

---

## Preconditions / access
You need:
- Access to **Control Plane feature gates** and runtime config (prod breakglass if applicable)
- Dashboard access (Kernel Selection v2 Rollout dashboards)
- Log access for serving runtime pods

Tools referenced:
- `rwctl` (Redwood internal CLI)
- Runtime admin endpoint (read-only + safe config reload)

If `rwctl` is unavailable, use the Control Plane Console: **Console → Runtime → Feature Gates**.

---

## Definitions
- **v1**: existing kernel selection behavior (baseline)
- **v2**: kernel selection logic keyed on model family + sequence regime + GPU SKU
- **Gate**: enable/disable selector v2
- **Allowlist / denylist**: model- or SKU-scoped enablement rules
- **Pin**: force a specific kernel choice (override), bypassing selector ranking

### Canonical identifiers
Use canonical forms to avoid mismatches:
- **Region:** `us-east-1`, `us-west-2`, `eu-central-1`
- **GPU SKU:** normalized string e.g. `nvidia-a100-80gb`, `nvidia-h100-sxm`, `nvidia-l40s`
- **Model ID:** `llama-3-70b-instruct`, `mistral-large-2407`, `qwen2-72b-instruct`, `gemma-2-27b-it`

If SKU naming is ambiguous (MIG / cloud instance mapping), see: "GPU SKU normalization" in the debugging playbook.

---

## Quick decision tree (2 minutes)
1) **Is this isolated to one model OR one SKU OR one region?**
   - Yes → Disable v2 narrowly (model/SKU/region) OR pin kernel
   - No → Disable v2 at environment scope (Hosted prod or pool-wide) and page Runtime Kernels

2) **Are there runtime errors (not just latency)?**
   - Yes → Prefer **denylisting** the kernel/SKU combination (or disabling v2 for that SKU) rather than pinning.

3) **Is there a customer impact in Dedicated/Private?**
   - Yes → Prefer **pool-specific** disable or pin; avoid global Hosted changes unless needed.

---

## Primary levers
You have four safe mitigation levers (in preferred order):
1) **Disable v2 for a model in a region** (least blast radius)
2) **Disable v2 for a GPU SKU in a region/pool**
3) **Pin a kernel for a model+SKU+seq bucket** (fast workaround, higher risk)
4) **Disable v2 globally** (largest blast radius; requires notification)

---

## Step 0 — Confirm it is selector v2
Before changing gat

hits.title: Cross-sku MIG clock interlock: kernel prioritization and attention tiling for H100/L40S/A10
hits.text:
description:
Background: multi-tenant inference workloads on H100/L40S/A10 show volatile tail latency during MIG consolidation and clock domain shifts. Current kernel selection heuristics assume static clock/perf profiles and do not account for transient P2P/NVLink contention or mixed quantized/FP16 execution paths. Goal: implement a cross-sku clock-interlock and kernel prioritization layer plus an attention-tiling policy that adapts prefill/decode scheduling to MIG partitioning and real-time clock governors. Success metrics: 95th percentile latency reduction of 15-25% on mixed small/long-sequence workloads across MIG partitions; token cost neutral or improved; no regression in throughput for long-batch offline workloads.

acceptance_criteria:
Kernel router uses live clock and MIG fragmentation signals to rank candidate kernels before scheduling
Attention tiler adjusts tile size and KV alignment to reduce L2 thrash on L40S without increasing decode latency > 5%
Prefill/decode interleave window introduced to avoid clock-rebalance stalls during MIG reconfigure and reduces 95th latency by >=15% in benchmark suite
Automated telemetry demonstrates correct fallback to a quantized-kernel-fusion path on A10 when H100/L40S capacity constrained
End-to-end e2e perf tests and canary on dedicated pool show no increase in error rate or CPU OOMs

work_notes:
2025-01-18: RFC written; linked design doc with microbenchmarks. Trade-offs considered: aggressive prefill batching vs latency-sensitive interleaving. Decision: hybrid interleaving with dynamic cutover thresholds.
2025-01-22: Infra experiment on staging with synthetic chat workload; observed 28% 95th latency spike when MIG fragmentation >60% during background training noise.
2025-01-25: Implemented clock-interlock event listener in runtime and exposed telemetry flag runtime.clock_interlock.enabled (off by default).
2025-01-29: Prototyped kernel-ranking heuristic that weights (kernel_peak_bw, current_device_clock, nvlink_util, mig_fragment_score). Initial synthetic results: 12% 95th reduction on H100-only trials.
2025-02-01: L40S attention tiler patch submitted; adjusts attn_tile to favor smaller tiles when L2 miss rate > 18%. PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4921
2025-02-03: End-to-end benchmark ran against mixed H100/L40S/A10 pool with prefill+decode interleave window set to 40ms; 95th improved by 17% and token cost decreased 3% on median. Noted small throughput regression on long-batch profiles (~4%).
Next steps: add NVLink P2P fallback handshake to kernel router; integrate autoswitch thresholds from telemetry; create canary rollout plan for dedicated customers and a gated feature flag for runtime-1.21 release.

risks_and_mitigations:
Risk: aggressive kernel switching can increase warmup overhead. Mitigation: add hysteresis and min residency time per kernel selection.
Risk: L40S micro-tiling may regress throughput on long static batches. Mitigation: enable tiler only when L2 miss + latency SLO signals are present.
Risk: MIG reconfigure race during runtime may cause transient errors. Mitigation: gate reconfigure events via interlock and drain inflight prefill windows before topology changes.

qa_plan:
Add unit tests for kernel router ranking weights and simulated clock events
Run full perf suite on multi-sku lab (H100/L40S/A10) with and without background NVSwitch load
Canary rollout to dedicated pool group 'perf-canary-02' with telemetry thresholds for automatic rollback

What success looks like:
- Lower p95/p99 latency + improved throughput stability on heterogeneous fleets (A100/H100/L40S).
- Zero correctness regressions; deterministic selection under identical inputs.
- Safe staged rollout with rapid rollback and per-model/per-region overrides.

Slide 3 — Scope: what’s in 1.21
Core runtime changes:
- v2 selector decision logic + interface updates (candidate generation, scoring/rules, fallback).
- Model-family classifier integration (architecture tags / variants).
- Seq-length bucketing + prefill/decode regime heuristics.
- GPU SKU-aware kernel registry + normalization (including variants/MIG where applicable).
- Guardrail: auto-disable v2 on known-unstable driver/CUDA combos.

Ops / safety:
- Feature gate plumbing (environment/region/model allowlist + denylist, hot reload).
- Oncall tooling: force kernel, dump selection trace, pin/override.
- Deterministic replay tests wired into CI.

Observability:
- Per-request selection telemetry events (sampled) + aggregated metrics.
- Rollout dashboards: selection distribution + latency deltas + error rate correlation.

Out of scope (explicitly NOT in 1.21):
- Learned selection model / ML-based scoring.
- Automatic cross-region failover policies driven by selection output (kept separate).
- Any default-on behavior across all hosted traffic.

Slide 4 — Kernel auto-selection v2: key highlights (talk track)
Problem statement (v1):
- v1 selection is insufficiently SKU-aware and under-reacts to long-context regimes.
- Tail latency spikes observed when long-context workloads are misclassified or when kernels behave differently across drivers.

v2 improvements:
- Feature signals: (1) model family/architecture (Llama/Mistral/Qwen/Gemma/variants), (2) seq bucket / regime hints, (3) GPU SKU.
- Decision rules are explicit + debuggable; telemetry captures “why” (features + candidate set).
- Fallback hierarchy prevents hard failures when a preferred kernel is missing/unstable.
- Determinism: selection depends only on declared inputs; replay tests guarantee identical selection.

Slide 5 — Config / gates (how we control blast radius)
Gate layers (evaluated in order):
1) Global gate: kernel_selection_v2.enabled (per env)
2) Driver/CUDA guardrail gate: kernel_selection_v2.blocked_driver_versions
3) GPU SKU allow/deny: kernel_selection_v2.gpu_sku_rules
4) Model allowlist/denylist: kernel_selection_v2.model_rules
5) Region/cluster policy: kernel_selection_v2.region_rules
6) Manual override: forced kernel / disable v2 via runtime flags (for debugging)

Default posture for GA:
- Enabled only for explicit allowlisted model families + GPU SKUs in hosted canary clusters.
- Dedicated/Private: opt-in only (customer readiness review required).

Slide 6 — Rollout plan (staged)
Phase 0 — Preflight (complete/ongoing):
- Merge behind gates + CI determinism tests
- Dashboards live + sampling policy validated
- Bench matrix coverage complete for key model families + seq distributions + SKUs

Phase 1 — Hosted canary (Week 1):
- 1 region, 1–2 canary clusters
- Allowlist: 1–2 model families, conservative seq buckets
- Monitor: selection distribution, p95/p99, errors, fallback rate

Phase 2 — Hosted expansion (Week 2):
- Add 1–2 regions; expand allow

Runtime **1.21** introduces **Kernel Auto-Selection v2** ("selector v2") for GPU inference kernels. The selector chooses the best available kernel **per request** using a deterministic, explainable rule-based policy keyed on:

This release is focused on reducing **p95/p99 latency** and improving **throughput stability** across heterogeneous fleets without correctness regressions.

New per-request telemetry is available (sampling-controlled) to support debugging and rollout monitoring:
- chosen kernel
- candidate set (capped)
- feature vector (model family, seq bucket, gpu sku)
- fallback reason (if applicable)

- Force kernel selection for reproductions and customer escalations.

[01:10] Omar El-Sayed: Sure. So, in our runtime we have multiple kernel implementations for key parts of attention and related ops. Depending on model architecture and workload regime, different kernels win. Kernel auto-selection is the module that picks, for a given request, which kernel variant to run.

[01:27] Omar El-Sayed: In v2 specifically, we key selection on three buckets of signals: one, model family/architecture tags (like Llama-style vs Mistral-style, Qwen variants, Gemma-ish), two, sequence-length regime which we treat separately for prefill vs decode behavior, and three, GPU SKU, because H100 vs A100 vs L40S can change the winner.

[01:51] Priya Nair: When you say “request”, do you literally decide per request? Or per model load, like at startup?

[01:57] Yuki Sato: Good question. We decide at request time, but in practice we cache decisions. The selector outputs a decision based on a normalized feature vector. Most of those are stable for many requests: model id + gpu sku + seq bucket. So it’s more like “per regime,” not every time doing heavy computation.

[02:18] Danielle Chen: And your v1 did what?

[02:21] Yuki Sato: v1 was simpler, basically a mostly static mapping keyed on model class and a couple hard-coded thresholds. It didn’t account for SKU differences well, and it treated sequence length too coarsely. It worked for the middle of the distribution but we saw edge cases on long context.

[02:39] Omar El-Sayed: And also v1 had weaker observability. So when you got a latency spike, you couldn’t easily answer “which kernel did we pick” without attaching a profiler.

[02:49] Alex Romero: So v2 is rules? Or some ML thing?

[02:53] Yuki Sato: Rules. We debated a learned scorer, but for safety and explainability and rollback, we landed on rule-based with explicit fallbacks. It’s still a “scoring” concept internally, but it’s deterministic rules and precedence, not a trained model.

[03:10] Priya Nair: Deterministic… like, identical inputs always produce identical output kernel choice?

[03:15] Yuki Sato: Yes. Given the same model metadata, same GPU normalized SKU, same seq bucket inputs, you get the same selection. We’ve added replay tests to ensure that. We also version the rules so if we change thresholds, it’s tracked.

[03:30] Tom Bowers: What about multi-tenant? Like if another customer is running something weird, does it influence our selection?

[03:35] Omar El-Sayed: No. There’s no global learning. The only “dynamic” input can be scheduler hints about observed seq distribution, but those are local to the pool and still deterministic given the hint input. And you can disable that if you want.

[03:49] Ethan Park: Also from the control plane side, for Dedicated you can lock policy. You can say “always use v1 selector” or “use v2 only for these models.” There’s no cross-account mixing.

[04:01] Danielle Chen: Let’s go into the seq bucket thing. Because our problem is long context. How do you bucket?

[04:07] Yuki Sato: We extract prompt length (prefill tokens) and also we estimate expected decode length using either the max_tokens setting or observed from recent traffic. Then we classify into regimes.

[04:19] Yuki Sato: Simplifying a bit: short, medium, long context for prefill; and small vs large decode. For prefill, long context triggers kernels optimized for memory bandwidth and larger tile sizes. The key bug we saw in early testing was misclassifying “very long prompt, small decode” as “mixed,” which picked a kernel optimized for decode throughput but had worse prefill tail.

[04:42] Omar El-Sayed: And that’s exactly the p99 symptom: average ok, but at the long tail you get a 1.5x

description:
Issue summary
- Customer reports p99 latency regression for long-context summarization workloads immediately after we enabled Runtime 1.21 canary on their Dedicated pool. Regression appears only for long-context requests (>= ~16k prompt tokens) and only on NVIDIA L40S.

Impact
- Customer-visible tail latency increase on long-context routes.
- Reported baseline (Runtime 1.20 / selector v1): p99 ~4.8–5.4s @ ~20k prompt tokens, 256–512 decode tokens.
- After canary (Runtime 1.21 / selector v2 enabled): p99 ~8.9–10.6s for same workload; p50/p90 mostly unchanged.
- No correctness issues reported. Error rate stable.

Customer context
- Northwind Analytics uses Redwood Dedicated for long-context summarization (document ingestion + map-reduce style prompts). Workload is bursty but within reserved throughput.

Environment
- Dedicated pool: nw-analytics-ded-01
- Region: us-east
- GPU SKU: NVIDIA L40S (SM89)
- Driver/CUDA: 550.54.14 / CUDA 12.4
- Runtime: 1.21.0-canary.3
- Feature: Kernel auto-selection v2 enabled via canary gate for Llama family

Steps to reproduce (as reported)
1) Send chat.completions with large prompts (~16k–32k tokens) and max_output_tokens 256–512.
2) Observe p99 latency increase vs previous runtime.
3) Short prompts (<4k) appear unaffected.

Observed signals
- Regressions correlate with selector choosing a different prefill kernel under v2 for the LONG seq bucket on L40S.
- Telemetry shows increased time in prefill stage; decode stage stable.

Example request IDs (customer-provided)
- req_7f2d5c8f2d8a4e1e (2026-02-20 18:12:44Z)
- req_3c19a0d91fb44b26 (2026-02-20 18:17:09Z)

Initial hypothesis
- Mis-selection in v2 for long-context prefill on L40S (SKU mapping + seq-bucket thresholds) causing fallback to a kernel variant with worse long-context characteristics on SM89.

Logs/snippets (redacted)
- Selection trace (sampled):
  - model_family=llama
  - seq_bucket=LONG
  - gpu_sku=l40s_sm89
  - chosen_prefill_kernel=fa3_fused_prefill_sm89 (candidate_score=0.71)
  - fallback_prefill_kernel=fa2_triton_prefill_sm89
  - chosen_decode_kernel=fa2_decode_sm89
- Perf counters summary (internal): prefill_ms +62% at 20k prompt; decode_ms within +/-3%.

Requested outcome
- Immediate mitigation (restore previous tail latency) and a safe path to re-enable v2 once fixed/guarded.

content.title: Runtime 1.21 Release Notes: Kernel Auto-Selection v2
content.text:
n cost is in the **single-digit microseconds** range, and sampling-controlled telemetry overhead is negligible at default settings.

Performance regressions should be treated as a **P0** if they increase p99 tail latency beyond rollout budgets (see SLO gates / dashboards).

---

## Compatibility Notes
- Supported GPU families in rollout scope: **A100, H100, L40S**.
- MIG: supported, but SKU normalization is strict; ensure the runtime reports a normalized `gpu_sku` consistent with the control plane rules.
- Private deployments pinned to constrained GPU types should validate with the benchmark matrix before enabling v2 globally.

---

## Known Limitations / Risks
1) **Long-context misclassification risk (prefill-heavy)**
   - Very long prefill requests (e.g., summarization with large context windows) are sensitive to incorrect bucketing.
   - If you observe tail spikes concentrated in long-context routes, disable v2 for the affected model(s) and region, then collect selection traces.

2) **Driver/CUDA guardrails**
   - Selector v2 is automatically disabled on specific driver/CUDA combinations that have not completed validation.
   - If you are running a nonstandard driver stack (common in some on-prem installs), confirm you are not implicitly falling back to v1.

3) **Telemetry cardinality**
   - New fields can increase metric cardinality if dashboards are queried without the recommended grouping limits.
   - Follow the dashboard spec for safe group-bys (model family / SKU / seq bucket) and avoid raw model-id group-bys unless sampled and capped.

4) **Kernel availability differences by SKU**
   - Some optimized kernels are SKU-specific. v2’s fallback rules are explicit, but you may see different kernel distributions between A100 and H100 under identical traffic.

---

## Rollout / Enablement Guidance
Recommended staged rollout order:
1. Enable v2 in **Hosted canary** for a small model allowlist.
2. Expand allowlist by model family + SKU cohorts (monitor p95/p99 and error rates).
3. Enable in **Dedicated pools** with explicit customer opt-in and documented rollback contact.
4. Promote to broader GA once SLO gates are green for at least one full traffic cycle.

Default enablement approach:
- Start with `kernel_selection.v2.model_allowlist` and keep a conservative denylist for known-sensitive long-context models until validated.

---

## Rollback Instructions (Fast Path)
If you suspect a latency regression, elevated error rate, or unexpected kernel distribution shift, roll back v2 using the smallest-scoped change that resolves impact.

### Hosted / Dedicated (control plane gate)
1. Disable v2 for the affected scope (start with model + region):
   - Set `kernel_selection.v2.enabled=false` (scoped) OR remove the model from the v2 allowlist.
2. Confirm hot reload applied:
   - Verify the selector mode in runtime logs: `kernel_selection_mode=v1` (or `v2 disabled by gate`).
3. Validate recovery:
   - Monitor p95/p99 latency and error rate panels in the Kernel Selection v2 rollout dashboards.
   - Confirm kernel distribution shifts back to expected v1 baselines.

### Private (customer-managed runtime config)
1. Set `kernel_selection.v2.enabled=false` and/or `kernel_selection.mode=v1` in `runtime.yaml`.
2. Restart the runtime service (or reload config if supported in the deployment).
3. Validate with the customer’s canary route:
   - Compare p99 latency for long-context traffic before/after.

### If immediate mitigation is required
- Pin a kernel only as a temporary measure:
  - Use `--force-kernel=<kernel_id>` (or equivalent config) for the impacted route/model while investigating.
  - Open a follow-up issue to remove the pin once denylist or thresholds are corrected.

---

## Troubleshooting Checklist
When filing an issue or escalating to oncall/runtime-kernels, include:
- Model id + model family
- GPU SKU (normalized) + whether MIG is used
- Driver/CUDA version tuple
- Workload description (prefill-heavy vs decode-heavy; typical context lengths)
- Selection traces (`--dump-kernel-selection`) for 20–50 representative requests
- Dashboard links: latency deltas + selection distribution by SKU/seq bucket

---

- Runtime Kernels: **Hiro Tanaka**, **Yuki Sato**
- Perf/correctness guardrails: **Noah Patel**
- Tail latency + observability: **Omar El-Sayed**, **Allison Grant**
- Control-plane feature gates: **Ethan Park**
- Release train: **Connor O'Brien**

For operational procedures and scoped overrides, follow: **Kernel Selection v2 Override and Rollback Runbook** (linked above).

hits.title: Kernel Auto-Selection v2 — Override and Rollback Runbook
hits.text:
## Purpose
This runbook describes how oncall can safely override or roll back **Kernel Auto-Selection v2** ("selector v2") when it causes tail-latency regressions, stability issues, or correctness risks. It covers:
- Disabling v2 by **model**, **GPU SKU**, and/or **region** (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)
- Pinning a specific kernel (temporary mitigation)
- Safe rollback procedure (fast + staged)
- Validation steps using dashboards and logs

**Primary goals:** restore p95/p99 latency and error rates to baseline while preserving correctness and preventing fleet-wide disruption.

---

## Scope / when to use
Use this runbook when any of the following are true during canary or production:
- p99 latency regression attributed to kernel selection (common: long-context prefill misclassification)
- Elevated runtime errors (CUDA illegal memory access, miscompiled kernel, launch failures) correlated with a chosen kernel/SKU
- Throughput instability or jitter that correlates with selection distribution changes
- Customer escalation requiring immediate mitigation (Dedicated/Private pools with constrained SKUs)

**Do not use** this runbook for general GPU/node instability, scheduler overload, or non-kernel runtime crashes unless kernel selection has been implicated.

---

## Ownership / escalation
**Oncall owns mitigation**, Runtime Kernels owns root cause.

- Runtime Oncall: #eng-oncall (primary)
- Runtime Kernels: #eng-runtime (paging if rollback required)
- SRE: #eng-sre (paging if SLO breach / incident)
- Releases: #eng-releases (if changes impact runtime 1.21 rollout windows)

Escalate immediately if:
- Any correctness regression suspected (bad outputs, determinism broken)
- Crash-looping exceeds 2% of pods in a region/pool
- You need to disable v2 globally in Hosted prod

---

## Preconditions / access
You need:
- Access to **Control Plane feature gates** and runtime config (prod breakglass if applicable)
- Dashboard access (Kernel Selection v2 Rollout dashboards)
- Log access for serving runtime pods

Tools referenced:
- `rwctl` (Redwood internal CLI)
- Runtime admin endpoint (read-only + safe config reload)

If `rwctl` is unavailable, use the Control Plane Console: **Console → Runtime → Feature Gates**.

---

## Definitions
- **v1**: existing kernel selection behavior (baseline)
- **v2**: kernel selection logic keyed on model family + sequence regime + GPU SKU
- **Gate**: enable/disable selector v2
- **Allowlist / denylist**: model- or SKU-scoped enablement rules
- **Pin**: force a specific kernel choice (override), bypassing selector ranking

### Canonical identifiers
Use canonical forms to avoid mismatches:
- **Region:** `us-east-1`, `us-west-2`, `eu-central-1`
- **GPU SKU:** normalized string e.g. `nvidia-a100-80gb`, `nvidia-h100-sxm`, `nvidia-l40s`
- **Model ID:** `llama-3-70b-instruct`, `mistral-large-2407`, `qwen2-72b-instruct`, `gemma-2-27b-it`

If SKU naming is ambiguous (MIG / cloud instance mapping), see: "GPU SKU normalization" in the debugging playbook.

---

## Quick decision tree (2 minutes)
1) **Is this isolated to one model OR one SKU OR one region?**
   - Yes → Disable v2 narrowly (model/SKU/region) OR pin kernel
   - No → Disable v2 at environment scope (Hosted prod or pool-wide) and page Runtime Kernels

2) **Are there runtime errors (not just latency)?**
   - Yes → Prefer **denylisting** the kernel/SKU combination (or disabling v2 for that SKU) rather than pinning.

3) **Is there a customer impact in Dedicated/Private?**
   - Yes → Prefer **pool-specific** disable or pin; avoid global Hosted changes unless needed.

---

## Primary levers
You have four safe mitigation levers (in preferred order):
1) **Disable v2 for a model in a region** (least blast radius)
2) **Disable v2 for a GPU SKU in a region/pool**
3) **Pin a kernel for a model+SKU+seq bucket** (fast workaround, higher risk)
4) **Disable v2 globally** (largest blast radius; requires notification)

---

## Step 0 — Confirm it is selector v2
Before changing gat

## 事件与影响
- 待核查：本稿供人工交接，不构成恢复结论；当前部署、遥测和健康状态不可见，用户所报“开启 v2 后 p99 回退”尚不能确认为本次根因。
- 历史工单：2026-02-20，Northwind Analytics 的 nw-analytics-ded-01（us-east），NVIDIA L40S/SM89、550.54.14/CUDA 12.4、Runtime 1.21.0-canary.3。约20k prompt、256–512 decode tokens 下，p99 从1.20/v1的约4.8–5.4s升至8.9–10.6s；影响≥约16k prompt，<4k基本不受影响，p50/p90、错误率基本稳定，未报告正确性问题。[E16]
## 原因与证据
- 历史1%采样显示 LONG/L40S 约78%选择 fa3_fused_prefill_sm89，v1基线为 fa2_triton_prefill_sm89；20k prompt 的 prefill_ms +62%，decode_ms 在±3%内，池利用率、排队和节点限流检查正常。支持选择路径相关性，不证明当前同因。[E16]
- 2026-02-21推测 LONG 分类阈值及SM89上fa3评分过激，550.54.14/CUDA 12.4交互仍属可能；2/22临时RCA归于L40S长prefill选择。此前H100优先POC与L40S事件范围不同，不能以H100/A100表现替代L40S验证。[E16][E12]
## 已采取的缓解
- 2026-02-20 20:41Z记录：该池 llama-3.1-70b-instruct、llama-3.1-8b-instruct 禁用v2，约90s热重载；增加 l40s_sm89 AND LONG 禁选 fa3_fused_prefill_sm89。pin fa2仅为“若支持”的提议，未见执行确认。[E16]
- 21:10Z客户确认约10分钟内改善，18–22k prompt 的p99约5.3–5.8s，无新错误；工单称回到基线，但数值并非严格等同此前4.8–5.4s，不能据此认定今天已恢复。[E16]
## 核查与恢复条件
- 由接手工程师核对目标实例日志确为v1/被gate禁用、热重载及deny命中；按SKU/seq bucket比较p95/p99、错误率和kernel分布是否回归v1，区分prefill/decode。补20–50条代表请求trace、ID/时间、长度直方图、输出上限、并发及MIG状态；这些是核查建议，非已执行。[E17][E16]
- Northwind窄条件：客户deny保留至1.21 GA；确认pr-28522落地、1.21.1发布且部署，L40S长上下文基准绿色、该驱动组合完成验证，才安排本池30–60 min受控canary；LONG p99回退>10%即回滚，须明确窗口及看板。[E16]
- 通用Dedicated启用还需客户明确opt-in及记录回滚联系人；推广GA要求SLO gates至少一个完整流量周期绿色。这些不替代上述客户条件；H100 POC提出的30 min、p99≤基线+3%、错误不增、分布稳定，也不能套作L40S重启阈值。[E17][E12]
## 未知与交接
- 待核查：当前版本、模型、池/区域、驱动/CUDA、gate/deny/pin实际状态及实时遥测；当前是否仍存在长prefill回退，或排队/饱和等其他原因。
- 待核查：补丁发布部署及本池canary结果、客户就绪确认、回滚联系人/窗口；现有记录只有内部验证与安排测试计划，无当前批准、完成证据或ETA。[E16][E17]
- 标识须核对，不可直接改写：工单使用us-east、l40s_sm89及上述3.1模型ID，runbook示例为us-east-1、nvidia-l40s、llama-3-70b-instruct；需确认实际控制面映射避免规则漏匹配。[E16][E19]

note: 片段来源检查通过不等于结论正确。该简报须人工复核，未连接现场监控或执行处置。
